title: Digest Outside, Fuse in Two Steps

scenes.visual: THE WORLD for both films (16:9, dark navy background, flat cartoon style, no molecular structures). Colour map, fixed: BACTERIA are BLUE, ARCHAEA (including methanogens) are ORANGE, EUKARYOTES (yeast, fungi, protists, animals, plants) are GREEN. Ribosomal RNA strands are drawn as a WHITE ribbon of small beads. Similarity scores are white numbers in grid cells; any tree or grid not computed from real data carries a small corner label 'schematic'. Same colour map as the first film: fungi are GREEN (eukaryotes). In this film, the two mating partners' nuclei are drawn as RED and YELLOW dots; a fused diploid nucleus is ORANGE-RED with both colours swirled. Bread is beige, starch is drawn as long white bead chains, small sugars as single white beads. Title card 'Digest Outside, Fuse in Two Steps' over a slice of bread with faint green fuzz.

scenes.tts: Sequences put fungi closer to animals than to plants. Yet a fungus eats like neither. So how does a mould on bread eat, with no mouth and no gut?
scenes.visual: A small inset tree in the corner, labelled 'schematic': GREEN twigs 'fungi' and 'animals' side by side, 'plants' further off. The inset shrinks as a slice of bread with a patch of green mould fills the screen; a question mark over the mould.
scenes.narration: Sequences put fungi closer to animals than to plants. Yet a fungus eats like neither. So how does a mould on bread eat, with no mouth and no gut?

scenes.tts: Watch a spore land on the bread. It grows a single thread, called a hypha. The hypha branches again and again into a mass called a mycelium. That fuzz is the mould.
scenes.visual: A green spore lands on the bread surface and sprouts one green thread, labelled 'hypha'. The thread branches repeatedly, spreading through the bread like roots, until the network is labelled 'mycelium'. Pull back to show the fuzzy patch on the slice.
scenes.narration: Watch a spore land on the bread. It grows a single thread, called a hypha. The hypha branches again and again into a mass called a mycelium. That fuzz is the mould.

scenes.tts: Each thread is wrapped in a wall that contains chitin, a tough polymer also found in insect exoskeletons. Fungi do not photosynthesize. So this mould's food must come from the bread.
scenes.visual: Cross-section of one hypha: a green tube with a thick outer line labelled 'wall: contains chitin'. A small beetle icon appears beside it with 'chitin' also on its shell. A sun icon with a red cross: 'no photosynthesis'.
scenes.narration: Each thread is wrapped in a wall that contains chitin, a tough polymer also found in insect exoskeletons. Fungi do not photosynthesize. So this mould's food must come from the bread.

scenes.tts: At the growing tip, the hypha releases enzymes into the bread. The enzymes cut starch, a large molecule, into small sugars outside the fungus. Then the hypha takes the sugars in.
scenes.visual: Close-up of a hyphal tip. Small yellow wedge shapes labelled 'enzymes' stream out of the tip into the bread. They snip long white bead chains labelled 'starch' into single white beads labelled 'small sugars'. The beads flow back into the hypha through its surface.
scenes.narration: At the growing tip, the hypha releases enzymes into the bread. The enzymes cut starch, a large molecule, into small sugars outside the fungus. Then the hypha takes the sugars in.

scenes.tts: So a fungus digests first and takes food in second. Most animals do the reverse. They take food into a gut, and digest it there.
scenes.visual: Split screen. Left: the hypha, arrows 'digest outside' then 'absorb'. Right: a simple cartoon animal with a tube gut, arrows 'take in' then 'digest inside'. The order of the two arrows is mirrored.
scenes.narration: So a fungus digests first and takes food in second. Most animals do the reverse. They take food into a gut, and digest it there.

scenes.tts: A thin thread suits this way of eating. Every part of its cytoplasm stays close to the surface where the food comes in.
scenes.visual: The hypha in cross-section; short arrows run from the surface to every point inside, labelled 'shorter transport distance'. Beside it, a fat round blob of the same material in grey, with longer arrows reaching its centre, labelled 'longer transport distance'. Both sets of arrows arrive; transport is slower in the blob, not impossible.
scenes.narration: A thin thread suits this way of eating. Every part of its cytoplasm stays close to the surface where the food comes in.

scenes.tts: Some fungi skip the threads. A yeast is a single cell. Baker's yeast reproduces by budding, pinching a small daughter cell off a larger one.
scenes.visual: A single oval GREEN cell labelled 'yeast'. A small bump grows on one side, swells and pinches off as a smaller daughter cell, labelled 'budding'.
scenes.narration: Some fungi skip the threads. A yeast is a single cell. Baker's yeast reproduces by budding, pinching a small daughter cell off a larger one.

scenes.tts: Now, how many fungi mate. Two hyphae of different mating types grow toward each other and meet. Their cytoplasm joins. This step is called plasmogamy.
scenes.visual: The bread fades away; a corner label appears and stays for the rest of the mating scenes: 'schematic: a cycle found in many fungi'. Two GREEN hyphae approach from left and right; one carries a RED nucleus dot, the other a YELLOW one; small tags 'mating type 1' and 'mating type 2'. Their tips touch and the boundary between them dissolves; one shared cytoplasm. Label 'plasmogamy: cytoplasm joins'.
scenes.narration: Now, how many fungi mate. Two hyphae of different mating types grow toward each other and meet. Their cytoplasm joins. This step is called plasmogamy.

scenes.tts: Each partner brought a haploid nucleus, carrying one set of chromosomes. Now the joined cell holds both nuclei, one from each partner, side by side.
scenes.visual: Inside the joined cell, the RED and YELLOW nuclei sit apart, each labelled 'haploid: 1 set'. A small counter in the corner reads 'sets of chromosomes in this cell: 2'.
scenes.narration: Each partner brought a haploid nucleus, carrying one set of chromosomes. Now the joined cell holds both nuclei, one from each partner, side by side.

scenes.tts: Two sets of chromosomes, in one cell. So is this cell diploid? Think about where the two sets are.
scenes.visual: Hold the cell with the red and yellow nuclei. On-screen question: 'Is this cell diploid?'
scenes.narration: Two sets of chromosomes, in one cell. So is this cell diploid? Think about where the two sets are.

scenes.visual: Hold the frame. A small pause icon and a countdown ring in the corner.

scenes.tts: Not yet. A diploid nucleus holds both sets in one nucleus. Here the two sets sit in two separate nuclei. A cell like this is called a dikaryon. In mushroom-forming fungi, this stage can last a long time.
scenes.visual: A red cross over the word 'diploid'. The two nuclei pulse, still separate. Label 'dikaryon: two separate haploid nuclei'. Then a tag 'in mushroom-forming fungi, this stage lasts long': the hypha grows on, and each new cell carries one red and one yellow nucleus.
scenes.narration: Not yet. A diploid nucleus holds both sets in one nucleus. Here the two sets sit in two separate nuclei. A cell like this is called a dikaryon. In mushroom-forming fungi, this stage can last a long time.

scenes.tts: Only a later step fuses the two nuclei into one diploid nucleus. That step is karyogamy. Plasmogamy joins cells. Karyogamy joins nuclei.
scenes.visual: In one cell the RED and YELLOW nuclei drift together and merge into a single ORANGE-RED swirled nucleus labelled 'diploid: 2 sets in one nucleus'. Label 'karyogamy'. Two summary tags appear: 'plasmogamy = cells join', 'karyogamy = nuclei join'.
scenes.narration: Only a later step fuses the two nuclei into one diploid nucleus. That step is karyogamy. Plasmogamy joins cells. Karyogamy joins nuclei.

scenes.tts: Then meiosis follows, and the cycle comes back to where it began. It makes haploid spores, each carrying one set of chromosomes again.
scenes.visual: The swirled nucleus divides twice into four small haploid nuclei; each nucleus is mottled red and yellow, a reshuffled mix of the two parents' chromosomes. Label 'meiosis', and a small tag 'spore number and packaging vary among fungi'. Spores bud off around the nuclei, drift away and land on soil, ready to grow new hyphae.
scenes.narration: Then meiosis follows, and the cycle comes back to where it began. It makes haploid spores, each carrying one set of chromosomes again.

scenes.tts: So a fungus eats by digesting outside itself and absorbing what it frees. And it mates in two steps. Cells fuse first, and nuclei later.
scenes.visual: A timeline across the screen: spore, hypha, enzymes out, sugars in; then plasmogamy, dikaryon, karyogamy, meiosis, spores. The two fusion steps glow.
scenes.narration: So a fungus eats by digesting outside itself and absorbing what it frees. And it mates in two steps. Cells fuse first, and nuclei later.

scenes.visual: End card with the Hex mascot beside a green hypha. Line: 'Fungi digest outside, absorb, and fuse cells before nuclei.'
